question.text: Which type of bond will have its Macaulay duration equal to its remaining maturity?

explanation.text: The Logic: Duration is the weighted average term of a bond's cash flows. Only a zero-coupon bond has duration equal to its remaining maturity, because the entire cash flow occurs at maturity with no intermediate coupons to pull the weighted average forward. The Trap: For coupon-bearing bonds, earlier coupon payments reduce the weighted average time to receive cash flows, so duration is always less than maturity. Note: Perpetual bonds have no maturity date at all, so duration cannot be "equal to remaining maturity" in their case.
